purpose: Azithromycin is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, such as chest infections, ear infections, throat infections, sinus infections, and some sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia. It works only against bacteria, so it will not help with colds, flu, or other viral illnesses. Your doctor chose this antibiotic because it matches the type of infection you have.
how_it_works: Azithromycin works by stopping bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow and multiply. Think of it like cutting off the bacteria's food supply — without those proteins, they cannot survive or spread. Over time, your immune system then clears the remaining bacteria from your body.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach upset, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach pain. Some people also get a headache or feel a bit dizzy. Taking it with food can help reduce stomach discomfort.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have heart rhythm problems, liver disease, or kidney disease, as azithromycin may not be safe for you. It can rarely cause a serious heart rhythm change called QT prolongation. Also let your doctor know about all other medications you take, as some can interact with it. If you develop a severe rash, difficulty breathing, or yellowing of your skin or eyes, seek medical help right away. Do not skip doses or stop early, even if you feel better, or the infection may come back.
typical_dosing: A common adult dose is 500 mg on the first day, then 250 mg once a day for the next 4 days — this is often called a Z-Pak. For some infections like chlamydia, a single 1000 mg dose is given all at once. Your exact dose depends on your infection, so always follow what your doctor or pharmacist tells you. Try to take it at the same time each day.
